The sarcophagus was sealed and intact but, when opened, empty. Seal impressions in the deposit carry Khufu's name. Vyse also had the pit in the floor of the Subterranean Chamber deepened to about 11 m and excavated beneath the coffer in the King's Chamber, finding solid masonry and rock in both cases. [reference-observable-reality.md] Unsupported objects denser than air fall; stone, metal, wood and people do not float in air. Water flows downhill and finds its own level; it does not rise in an open channel without being pushed or pumped. Nothing lifts itself: raising a mass takes work from outside it. Heat flows from hot to cold; a cool room does not warm a hot one. Sound needs air or a solid to travel and gets quieter with distance; a sound that cannot be heard outside a wall was not heard outside the wall. Fire needs fuel, heat and air. Limestone and gypsum dissolve slowly in water; dry stone stays dry when kept from water. A sealed container does not lose its contents. The sun rises in the east and sets in the west; shadows point away from the sun and are longest near sunrise and sunset. A human cannot lift a tonne, breathe under water, or live without water for weeks. Light does not bend around corners in open air. A thing cannot be in two places at once. A machine with no moving parts does no mechanical work. A building that has stood for thousands of years was not built to collapse. Nothing on Earth, left to itself, moves faster than it was thrown, dropped, or driven.

[scanpyramids-2017.md] Three independent muon detection techniques (nuclear emulsion films placed in the Queen's Chamber, scintillator hodoscopes in the Queen's Chamber, and gas detectors outside the pyramid) detected a large void above the Grand Gallery. The void is at least 30 m long, with a cross-section similar to that of the Grand Gallery (about 8 m high), located between 50 and 70 m above ground. Its muon signal is comparable to that of the Grand Gallery, consistent with an empty (air-filled) space. Muon imaging records only material above the detector positions; the bedrock beneath the pyramid is outside the method's view from these positions. A later campaign (2023) confirmed the void and imaged a 9 m corridor behind the north face chevrons.

[edgar-1910.md] The Grotto is a natural cavity or fissure in the rock uncovered when the builders levelled the site; the well shaft passes through it, and the builders walled it with small courses of stone and packed it with sand and gravel as foundation fill. Investigators after Al Mamoun's time broke through the lower courses of its south wall, found only sand and gravel, and threw their spoil down the well, blocking its lower end. Wedged at the east edge of the deep hollow in the Grotto's floor lies a large granite stone of broken appearance, apparently a fragment of a larger block, with two worked surfaces at right angles to each other and parts of two large holes drilled through it.

[lehner-1985-hetepheres.md] Lehner argues that the shaft tomb G7000x east of the Great Pyramid, found by Reisner in 1925 with Hetepheres I's furniture, canopic chest and sealed but empty sarcophagus, was her original burial made under Khufu, and that Khufu later moved her body into the first of the queens' pyramids beside his own (G1-a) when it was built, leaving the shaft burial sealed. On this reading the empty sarcophagus was not the result of a robbery concealed from the king but of a reburial ordered by him.

[cole-1925.md] Cole's survey of the base from the recovered corner sockets and casing lines gives the side lengths: north 230.253 m, south 230.454 m, east 230.391 m, west 230.357 m; mean 230.364 m. The perimeter is therefore 921.455 m. The sides deviate from true north by about 3 arcminutes (north side 2' 28" west of north; the mean of the four sides about 3' 6"). Cole did not determine the height.

[edgar-1910.md] The large granite block found by Professor Flinders Petrie in the Descending Passage has a four-inch drill hole through it; the two next largest granite pieces also each have a pair of drill holes. The block lacks the projections and rebates of the Granite Leaf; Petrie's suggestion that it was a further portcullis from the Antechamber faces the objection that the grooves there are too wide. Its original purpose is unknown.

[edgar-1910.md] The well shaft descends about 125 feet below the Grotto; its inclined section is about 30 inches high and 22 to 25 inches wide, with rough footholds cut in the walls.

[lehner-1997.md] Great Pyramid of Khufu: base 230.33 m, original height 146.59 m, slope 51° 50' 40". Volume about 2.6 million cubic metres; roughly 2.3 million blocks. The King's Chamber, lined and roofed in granite, measures about 10.47 m by 5.23 m and is 5.84 m high; above it are five relieving chambers roofed with granite beams, the topmost gabled. The Queen's Chamber lies on the pyramid's central axis and has a corbelled niche in its east wall. The Grand Gallery is 47 m long and 8.6 m high. The chamber floors lie at roughly 43 m (King's) and 21 m (Queen's) above the base.

[petrie-1883.md] The coffer in the King's Chamber is 89.62 inches long, 38.50 inches wide and 41.31 inches high outside (2.276 m by 0.978 m by 1.049 m). It has a groove for a sliding lid along the top of three sides and three pin holes in the rim at the west end; the lid is absent. The coffer is wider than the Ascending Passage, so it was placed in the chamber during construction. Its surfaces show the marks of a saw and a tubular drill.

[scanpyramids-2017.md] Three independent muon detection techniques (nuclear emulsion films placed in the Queen's Chamber, scintillator hodoscopes in the Queen's Chamber, and gas detectors outside the pyramid) detected a large void above the Grand Gallery. The void is at least 30 m long, with a cross-section similar to that of the Grand Gallery (about 8 m high), located between 50 and 70 m above ground. Its muon signal is comparable to that of the Grand Gallery, consistent with an empty (air-filled) space. Muon imaging records only material above the detector positions; the bedrock beneath the pyramid is outside the method's view from these positions. A later campaign (2023) confirmed the void and imaged a 9 m corridor behind the north face chevrons.

[reisner-1927-hetepheres.md] Reisner reports the discovery in 1925 of a 30 m shaft (G7000x) east of the Great Pyramid containing the gilded furniture, inlaid boxes, canopic chest with preserved organs in natron solution, and the alabaster sarcophagus of Queen Hetepheres I, wife of Snefru and mother of Khufu. The sarcophagus was sealed and intact but, when opened, empty. Seal impressions in the deposit carry Khufu's name. Reisner proposed that her original tomb at Dahshur had been robbed and the body lost, and that officials reburied the surviving equipment at Giza without informing the king.

[vyse-1840.md] Vyse blasted upward from Davison's Chamber in 1837 and opened four further relieving chambers above the King's Chamber (named for Wellington, Nelson, Lady Arbuthnot and Campbell), the topmost gabled. In these sealed chambers he found quarry marks in red ochre, including cartouches of Khufu and the names of work gangs. Some of the marks run under the joints between blocks, showing they were painted before the blocks were set. Vyse also had the pit in the floor of the Subterranean Chamber deepened to about 11 m and excavated beneath the coffer in the King's Chamber, finding solid masonry and rock in both cases. [lehner-1985-hetepheres.md] Lehner argues that the shaft tomb G7000x east of the Great Pyramid, found by Reisner in 1925 with Hetepheres I's furniture, canopic chest and sealed but empty sarcophagus, was her original burial made under Khufu, and that Khufu later moved her body into the first of the queens' pyramids beside his own (G1-a) when it was built, leaving the shaft burial sealed.
